claim: Flow cytometry is one of the standards that offers a method to characterize and isolate cells at high throughput.
source: Flow cytometry is one of the standards that offers a method to characterize and isolate cells at high throughput.
evidence: This is a general statement about flow cytometry that is part of established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Molecular staining is costly and its chemical toxicity can cause side effects to the cells.
source: However, molecular staining is costly and its chemical toxicity can cause side effects to the cells which becomes a critical issue when the cells are used downstream as medical products or for further analysis.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section discussing disadvantages of molecular staining.

claim: iSGC uses machine learning to derive molecular labels from compressive data obtained with diffractive and scattering imaging methods.
source: Instead of detecting molecular stains, we use machine learning to derive the molecular labels from compressive data obtained with diffractive and scattering imaging methods.
evidence: This is a direct description of the method presented in the manuscript.

claim: iSGC was able to distinguish different cell states, cell types derived from human induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells, and subtypes of peripheral white blood cells using only stain-free modalities.
source: With this method, we were able to distinguish different cell states, cell types derived from human induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells, and subtypes of peripheral white blood cells using only stain-free modalities.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental results presented in Figures 2-5 of the manuscript.

claim: Molecular staining has numerous disadvantages including cost in terms of both time and money.
source: However, molecular staining has numerous disadvantages: the staining process is costly in terms of both time and money; number of detectable markers with fluorescence detection are limited by the spectral overlap of fluorophores (Perfetto et al., 2004); multiple spectral compensation is complex and time consuming (Roederer, 2001); immunocytochemistry staining is inconsistent due to the wide variability of antibodies (Burry, 2011; Weigert et al., 1970); and molecular staining potentially causes side effects to the cells by chemical toxicity (Fried et al., 1982; Patil et al., 2018; Progatzky et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The number of detectable markers with fluorescence detection are limited by the spectral overlap of fluorophores.
source: However, molecular staining has numerous disadvantages: the staining process is costly in terms of both time and money; number of detectable markers with fluorescence detection are limited by the spectral overlap of fluorophores (Perfetto et al., 2004); multiple spectral compensation is complex and time consuming (Roederer, 2001); immunocytochemistry staining is inconsistent due to the wide variability of antibodies (Burry, 2011; Weigert et al., 1970); and molecular staining potentially causes side effects to the cells by chemical toxicity (Fried et al., 1982; Patil et al., 2018; Progatzky et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Perfetto et al., 2004.

claim: Multiple spectral compensation is complex and time consuming.
source: However, molecular staining has numerous disadvantages: the staining process is costly in terms of both time and money; number of detectable markers with fluorescence detection are limited by the spectral overlap of fluorophores (Perfetto et al., 2004); multiple spectral compensation is complex and time consuming (Roederer, 2001); immunocytochemistry staining is inconsistent due to the wide variability of antibodies (Burry, 2011; Weigert et al., 1970); and molecular staining potentially causes side effects to the cells by chemical toxicity (Fried et al., 1982; Patil et al., 2018; Progatzky et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Roederer, 2001.

claim: Immunocytochemistry staining is inconsistent due to the wide variability of antibodies.
source: However, molecular staining has numerous disadvantages: the staining process is costly in terms of both time and money; number of detectable markers with fluorescence detection are limited by the spectral overlap of fluorophores (Perfetto et al., 2004); multiple spectral compensation is complex and time consuming (Roederer, 2001); immunocytochemistry staining is inconsistent due to the wide variability of antibodies (Burry, 2011; Weigert et al., 1970); and molecular staining potentially causes side effects to the cells by chemical toxicity (Fried et al., 1982; Patil et al., 2018; Progatzky et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burry, 2011 and Weigert et al., 1970.

claim: Molecular staining potentially causes side effects to the cells by chemical toxicity.
source: However, molecular staining has numerous disadvantages: the staining process is costly in terms of both time and money; number of detectable markers with fluorescence detection are limited by the spectral overlap of fluorophores (Perfetto et al., 2004); multiple spectral compensation is complex and time consuming (Roederer, 2001); immunocytochemistry staining is inconsistent due to the wide variability of antibodies (Burry, 2011; Weigert et al., 1970); and molecular staining potentially causes side effects to the cells by chemical toxicity (Fried et al., 1982; Patil et al., 2018; Progatzky et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fried et al., 1982; Patil et al., 2018; Progatzky et al., 2013.

claim: Recent studies revealed the potentiality of bridging between images and molecular labels through prediction of labels from imaging information or 'in silico labeling.'
source: Although unstained cell images were thought to lack specific biomolecular information, recent studies (Christiansen et al., 2018; Ounkomol et al., 2018) revealed the potentiality of bridging between images and molecular labels: prediction of labels from imaging information or 'in silico labeling.'
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Christiansen et al., 2018 and Ounkomol et al., 2018.

claim: Conventional microscope-based approaches utilizing in silico labeling sacrifice the high throughput and sorting capability which exist in molecular labeling methods.
source: However, these approaches utilizing conventional microscopes sacrifice the high throughput and sorting capability which exist in molecular labeling methods (Han et al., 2016; Lindström, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Han et al., 2016 and Lindström, 2012.

claim: The acquisition of microscopy images is slow, and the processing of high-content images is even slower.
source: This restriction arises from the fact that the acquisition of microscopy images is slow, and the processing of high-content images is even slower (Pepperkok and Ellenberg, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pepperkok and Ellenberg, 2006.

claim: Conventional flow-based cell sorting systems process simple cell information fast enough to operate at around 10,000 cells/s.
source: In contrast, conventional flow-based cell sorting systems that process simple cell information such as total fluorescence intensity fast enough to operate at around 10,000 cells/s (Sutermaster and Darling, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sutermaster and Darling, 2019.

claim: Ghost cytometry is an 'imaging' cytometry that is able to predict cell types based on fluorescence signals encoded with morphological information of cells.
source: Previously, we have demonstrated ghost cytometry, an 'imaging' cytometry that is able to predict cell types based on fluorescence signals encoded with morphological information of cells (Ota et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ota et al., 2018.

claim: Previous ghost cytometry required fluorescence staining.
source: However, the usage of fluorescence staining was inevitable and, therefore, could not suffice applications where cell staining is unfavorable.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the previous ghost cytometry method.

claim: iSGC performs ultrafast real-time prediction of biological labels by machine learning-based analysis of compressively measured image information of cells in a processing time of down to the order of microseconds on a field-programmable gate array (FPGA).
source: This method performs ultrafast real-time prediction of biological labels by machine learning-based analysis of compressively measured image information of cells in a processing time of down to the order of microseconds on a field-programmable gate array (FPGA).
evidence: This is a description of the method's performance characteristics.

claim: In iSGC, machine learning models are pre-trained by the stain-free imaging data and biological labels obtained by fluorescence staining.
source: Herein, the machine learning models are pre-trained by the stain-free imaging data and biological labels obtained by fluorescence staining; afterward, it becomes able to predict the biological labels without the measurement of fluorescence labeling.
evidence: This describes the training procedure of the method.

claim: An imaging waveform is obtained from cells passing through a structured illumination at a speed where the signal width is shorter than 100 µs.
source: Similar to previously reported fluorescence ghost cytometry (Ota et al., 2018), an imaging waveform is obtained from cells passing through a structured illumination at a speed where the signal width is shorter than 100 µs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a technical description of the method supported by reference to a figure.

claim: In iSGC, one to several fringe patterns in the diffractive speckle pattern from the transmitted light are acquired with a single-pixel detector.
source: However, instead of collecting the whole photons with a bucket detector, to perform stain-free imaging, one to several fringe patterns in the diffractive speckle pattern from the transmitted light are acquired with a single-pixel detector (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a technical aspect of the method with reference to a figure.

claim: iSGC adopts a reduced acquisition for performing high-speed cell classification.
source: While full image reconstruction was demonstrated either with iterative acquisition using different structured illuminations or structured masks with a single-pixel detector (Horisaki et al., 2017a; Horisaki et al., 2017b), iSGC adopts a reduced acquisition for performing high-speed cell classification (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the approach taken in iSGC with citations to related work.

claim: HeLa S3 cells and MIA PaCa-2 cells are similar in size.
source: The two cell lines are similar in size (Figure 2A) and mixed at equal concentration with only one of them stained with green fluorescence using LIVE/DEAD Fixable Green Dead Cell Stain (Invitrogen) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The actual time lapsed during the judgment for a single cell with the FPGA was 6.0 µs.
source: The actual time lapsed during the judgment for a single cell with the FPGA was 6.0 µs.
evidence: This is a direct measurement of processing time.

claim: iSGC was able to infer the fluorescence label corresponding to the cell type from a fluorescence-free measurement at a high area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.963 for cells flowed after training.
source: As a result, iSGC was able to infer the fluorescence label corresponding to the cell type in this first case from a fluorescence-free measurement at a high area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.963 for cells flowed after training (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C and D.

claim: iSGC classified the cells at an accuracy of 0.917 according to the FPGA classifier.
source: In the actual sorting process, iSGC classified the cells at an accuracy of 0.917 according to the FPGA classifier (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), and the purity of the actual sorted cells was 97.3% (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The purity of the actual sorted cells was 97.3%.
source: In the actual sorting process, iSGC classified the cells at an accuracy of 0.917 according to the FPGA classifier (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), and the purity of the actual sorted cells was 97.3% (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Using only FSC and SSC, the SVM-based classifier had an AUC of only 0.936±0.005.
source: Using only FSC and SSC, the SVM-based classifier can only draw a decision boundary in 2D space, and the classification had an AUC of only 0.936±0.005 (gray dashed line in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Using FSC and SSC, dead cells are distinguishable but apoptotic cells are difficult to distinguish from live cells at high accuracy.
source: It is known that using FSC and SSC (or FSC and BSC), dead cells are distinguishable but apoptotic cells are difficult to distinguish from live cells at high accuracy (Darzynkiewicz et al., 1992; Dive et al., 1992; Shapiro, 2005; Zamai et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Using dGMI and bsGMI modalities for iSGC, it was able to distinguish dead and apoptotic cells from live cells with an AUC of 0.998±0.002 and 0.877±0.007.
source: Using dGMI and bsGMI modalities for iSGC, it was able to distinguish dead and apoptotic cells from live cells with an AUC of 0.998±0.002 and 0.877±0.007 (Figure 3D,E blue solid lines in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D, E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Using the FSC and BSC data with the same labels for SVM-based classification, conventional flow cytometry can only achieve a limited performance of 0.973±0.007 and 0.779±0.011.
source: In contrast, using the FSC and BSC data with the same labels for SVM-based classification, conventional flow cytometry can only achieve a limited performance of 0.973±0.007 and 0.779±0.011 (gray dashed lines in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Using conventional gating in the FSC-BSC scatter plot, apoptotic cells cannot be excluded from live cells.
source: Especially, between apoptotic and live cells, both populations overlap in the FSC-BSC scatter plot (Figure 3C), and with conventional gating in the FSC-BSC scatter plot (Hawley and Hawley, 2004) (region within the red line in Figure 3B), apoptotic cells cannot be excluded from live cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3B and 3C and citation to Hawley and Hawley, 2004.

claim: Using iSGC, apoptotic cells can be distinguished from live cells within the conventional gate with an AUC of 0.891±0.012.
source: Using iSGC, we can distinguish apoptotic cells from live cells within this gate with an AUC of 0.891±0.012 (Figure 3F, blue solid line in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Remaining undifferentiated cells can eventually cause tumor formation after their transplantation.
source: This is critical because remaining undifferentiated cells can eventually cause the tumor formation after their transplantation (Ben-David and Benvenisty, 2011; Knoepfler, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ben-David and Benvenisty, 2011 and Knoepfler, 2009.

claim: Using dGMI and ssGMI waveforms, the classifier distinguished iPSCs and NECs with an AUC of 0.929±0.008.
source: Using dGMI and ssGMI waveforms of each cell type labeled by the undifferentiation marker as training data set, the classifier distinguished iPSCs and NECs with an AUC of 0.929±0.008 (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and iPSCs and HECs with an AUC of 0.942±0.007 (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), showing its high classification capability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Using dGMI and ssGMI waveforms, the classifier distinguished iPSCs and HECs with an AUC of 0.942±0.007.
source: Using dGMI and ssGMI waveforms of each cell type labeled by the undifferentiation marker as training data set, the classifier distinguished iPSCs and NECs with an AUC of 0.929±0.008 (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and iPSCs and HECs with an AUC of 0.942±0.007 (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), showing its high classification capability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Using only both FSC and SSC information, the AUCs for the SVM-based classification of iPSCs and NECs, and iPSCs and HECs were limited to 0.856±0.009 and 0.697±0.016.
source: In contrast, using only both FSC and SSC information, the AUCs for the SVM-based classification of each pair of cell types were limited to 0.856±0.009 and 0.697±0.016 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, D and E), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: RPE cells are the first iPSC-derived cells tested clinically.
source: We chose retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, the first iPSC-derived cells tested clinically, as a product of regenerative medicine (Cyranoski, 2017; Cyranoski, 2014; Garber, 2015; Mandai et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cyranoski, 2017; Cyranoski, 2014; Garber, 2015; Mandai et al., 2017.

claim: The AUC for classification of RPE cells with Y-79 cells was 0.994±0.002.
source: Using dGMI and ssGMI waveforms labeled based on the intensity of CellMask Green as training data set (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), the AUC for classification of RPE cells with Y-79 cells was 0.994±0.002 (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Using FSC and SSC information for the SVM-based classification of RPE cells with Y-79 cells, the AUC was limited to 0.966±0.004.
source: In contrast, simultaneously using FSC and SSC information for the SVM-based classification, the AUC was limited to 0.966±0.004 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: To achieve a false positive rate of less than 1%, 92% of the RPE cells can be recovered with iSGC but only 52% of the RPE cells can be recovered with FSC and SSC.
source: For instance, to achieve a false positive rate of less than 1%, 92% of the RPE cells can be recovered with iSGC but only 52% of the RPE cells can be recovered with FSC and SSC (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is derived from analysis of the ROC curves as described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Peripheral white blood cell (WBC) differential count is necessary for the diagnosis of diseases such as inflammatory states, sepsis, allergy, and hematologic malignancies.
source: For example, peripheral white blood cell (WBC) differential count is necessary for the diagnosis of diseases such as inflammatory states, sepsis, allergy, and hematologic malignancies (Blumenreich, 1990; Roussel et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blumenreich, 1990 and Roussel et al., 2012.

claim: The current reference method for WBC differential is a 400 cell count performed manually under a microscope.
source: The current reference method is a 400 cell count performed manually under a microscope (Cherian et al., 2010; Hubl et al., 1997; Roussel et al., 2012; Roussel et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cherian et al., 2010; Hubl et al., 1997; Roussel et al., 2012; Roussel et al., 2010.

claim: When classification was performed for two donors in an intra-donor manner, macro-average F1-scores of 0.906±0.003 and 0.906±0.002 were obtained.
source: When we performed the classification for two donors in an intra-donor manner by training a model using data from one donor and applying it to data from the same donor, macro-average F1-scores of 0.906±0.003 and 0.906±0.002 were obtained, respectively (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: When classification was performed for two donors in an inter-donor manner, macro-average F1-scores of 0.901±0.002 and 0.884±0.004 were obtained.
source: Moreover, when we performed the classification for the same two donors in an inter-donor manner by training a model using a data set from one donor and applying it to a data set from another donor, and vice versa, macro-average F1-scores of 0.901±0.002 and 0.884±0.004 were obtained, respectively (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The advantage of iSGC over conventional label-free flow cytometry modalities with a scalar quantity is that it measures more detailed information of cells for a more accurate cell selection.
source: The advantage of iSGC over conventional label-free flow cytometry modalities with a scalar quantity is that it measures more detailed information of cells for a more accurate cell selection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results comparing iSGC to conventional methods.

claim: With conventional FSC and SSC, each modality yields a single scaler value, and therefore, even combined, the gating is only in a 2D space.
source: For instance, with conventional FSC and SSC, each modality yields a single scaler value, and therefore, even combined, the gating is only in a 2D space.
evidence: This is a description of the limitations of conventional flow cytometry based on established knowledge.

claim: iSGC utilizes a waveform containing over 100 points and performs classification in this high-dimensional space.
source: However, iSGC utilizes a waveform containing over 100 points and performs classification in this high-dimensional space.
evidence: This is a description of the technical characteristics of the iSGC method.

claim: iSGC often shows poor classification performances when morphological differences are not easily visually recognizable between cells to be classified.
source: For example, iSGC often shows poor classification performances when morphological differences are not easily visually recognizable between cells to be classified.
evidence: This is a discussion of the limitations of the method based on the authors' experience.

claim: Differentiation of CD4 and CD8 T cells has been challenging to both ghost cytometry and visual inspection.
source: From our experiences, differentiation of CD4 and CD8 T cells are one example which have been challenging to both ghost cytometry and our eyes.
evidence: This is based on the authors' experimental experience.

claim: A model developed using different data can be applied to a new sample or application in general.
source: On the other hand, transferability of a model can be advantageous: a model developed using different data can be applied to a new sample or application in general, just as those using 2D images can be applied to a new sample or application.
evidence: This is a discussion of the potential advantages of the method based on inference from the results.

claim: The iSGC machine is currently equipped with a self-calibration system for controlling the position of flow streams of cells relative to the illumination pattern.
source: Moreover, the iSGC machine is currently equipped with a self-calibration system for controlling the position of flow streams of cells relative to the illumination pattern, which is analogous to a situation where objects come to the same position in the 2D images, consequently enhancing the robustness of models over a long time or between experiments.
evidence: This is a description of a technical feature of the system.

claim: The good results of inter-donor classification of the six cell types provide evidence for the robustness of models.
source: This is evidenced by the good results of inter-donor classification of the six cell types.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results of inter-donor classification.

claim: The concept of iSGC is not limited to the modalities used in this work—other label-free modalities with high dimensions can also be used and combined.
source: In addition to the modalities of conventional FSC and SSC, dGMI, fsGMI, bsGMI, ssGMI, and bfGMI, we used in this work, the concept of iSGC is not limited to those—other label-free modalities with high dimensions can also be used and combined.
evidence: This is a discussion of the potential extensibility of the method.

claim: Holographic measurements may be further compressed for classifying the cells based on iSGC.
source: In the case of holography, the reconstruction of the object image from compressive measurements have been demonstrated (Brady et al., 2009; Lim et al., 2011; Marim et al., 2010), These holographic measurements may be further compressed for classifying the cells based on iSGC.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications, supported by citations to prior work on holography.

claim: The potential applications of iSGC include purification and quality control of cell manufacturing products and diagnostic tests using blood cells.
source: The potential applications of this method are similar to those of other image-based cell classification, including purification and quality control of cell manufacturing products and diagnostic tests using blood cells, as we demonstrated in this work.
evidence: This is a discussion of potential applications based on the demonstrated results.

claim: The advantage of iSGC over conventional image-based cell classification is that iSGC is able to perform cell classification at higher throughputs.
source: The advantage over conventional image-based cell classification is that iSGC is able to perform cell classification at higher throughputs which is necessary for analyzing large populations of cells in manufacturing (Sutermaster and Darling, 2019) and in diagnostic tests where rare cell detection is often required.
evidence: This is a comparison to other methods with citation to support the importance of high throughput.

claim: In contrast to microscopy image-based cell classification, iSGC-based high-throughput enrichment of the desired cells allows their use for downstream uses in manufacturing as well as molecular assays in further detailed analysis.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to microscopy image-based cell classification, iSGC-based high-throughput enrichment of the desired cells allows us to use them for their downstream uses in manufacturing as well as molecular assays in further detailed analysis (Grün and van Oudenaarden, 2015).
evidence: This is a discussion of advantages with citation to support the importance of downstream analysis.

claim: The concept of iSGC can be used with a variety of ground truth labels.
source: Finally, the concept of iSGC can be used with a variety of ground truth labels.
evidence: This is a discussion of the flexibility of the method.

claim: Ground truth labels in training data sets can be prepared with various surface markers, genetic reporters, and functional assays.
source: Depending on the characteristics of cell populations and the purpose of classifications, ground truth labels in training data sets can be prepared with various surface markers, genetic reporters (Zhang et al., 2014), and functional assays (Barros et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a discussion of potential labeling strategies with citations to support the feasibility.

claim: Separated cell populations showing characteristics such as responder versus non-responder cells, or disease versus healthy cells, can be used as labels for training a model.
source: Furthermore, if we have separated cell populations showing characteristics such as responder versus non-responder cells (Belzeaux et al., 2012), or disease versus healthy cells, they can be used as a label training a model to classify and selectively sort the unknown cells.
evidence: This is a discussion of potential applications with citation to support the concept.

claim: One approach when molecular labels suitable as ground truth labels are unavailable is to use the same high-dimensional modalities for clustering cells based on morphological information via dimension reduction and then adopt these visualized clusters as new labels for training the supervised learning model in iSGC.
source: In addition, it is often the case that molecular labels suitable as ground truth labels are unavailable or less-biased clustering of the morphological information is preferred. One approach for this issue is to use the same high-dimensional modalities for clustering cells based on morphological information via dimension reduction and then adopt these visualized clusters as new labels for training the supervised learning model in iSGC.
evidence: This is a discussion of potential alternative approaches when labels are unavailable.

claim: iSGC is a high-speed, stain-free cytometry that predicts labels based on compressive imaging information without image reconstruction.
source: In conclusion, we have developed a high-speed, stain-free cytometry that predicts labels based on compressive imaging information without image reconstruction.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the method developed in the manuscript.

claim: This staining-free technology will find its applications in a wide range of medical fields such as cell manufacturing in regenerative cell therapy and blood cell enumeration and differentiation in clinical diagnosis.
source: This staining-free technology will find its applications in a wide range of medical fields such as cell manufacturing in regenerative cell therapy and blood cell enumeration and differentiation in clinical diagnosis.
evidence: This is a discussion of potential future applications based on the demonstrated capabilities.

claim: The key to this technology is in turning imaging modalities that are incomprehensible to humans practical for cell characterization by using machine learning to correlate them to biological labels.
source: The key to this technology is in turning imaging modalities that are incomprehensible to humans practical for cell characterization by using machine learning to correlate them to biological labels.
evidence: This is a conceptual summary of the approach taken in the manuscript.
